en-US.title: Value creation
en-US.description:
**Producing benefits that exceed the resources and burdens involved.**

### Reasoning through the example

Compare the repair with what would happen otherwise. Suppose replacement uses relevant resources worth 100, while a repair of equal expected usefulness uses resources worth 30 and customer time worth 10. The simplified net saving is 60. A repair fee divides that benefit between customer and shop rather than adding another physical resource saving. If the repaired device fails sooner, or disposal harms are omitted, the comparison must change; the assumed equal usefulness matters.

### Reasoning through the example

Compare the repair with what would happen otherwise. Suppose replacement would cost 100, while a repair of equal expected usefulness uses resources worth 30 and customer time worth 10. The simplified net saving is 60. A repair fee divides that benefit between customer and shop rather than adding another physical resource saving. If the repaired device fails sooner, or disposal harms are omitted, the comparison must change; the assumed equal usefulness matters.

### Conditions

Specify whose benefits, costs, time horizon and alternatives matter.

### Example

Repairing a device avoids replacement costs and waste.

### Watch out

Revenue growth alone does not establish greater social value.

en-US.title: Systems perspective
en-US.description:
**Understanding organizational results through interactions and feedback among parts.**

### Reasoning through the example

Suppose intake accepts twelve cases per hour while processing completes eight. With no losses or other exits, the waiting backlog grows by four each hour. Making intake faster can therefore worsen overall waiting unless processing capacity or arrival patterns also change. Count completed cases across the whole path rather than celebrating one station’s speed. Real systems may have rework and delayed effects, so specify what enters, leaves and returns before attributing a bottleneck.
